assumptions: That the 13:45Z deploy actually reached the traffic that degraded — no verification was done beyond it appearing in the change log.

That the change log and the flag provider's history are complete for the service; 'no recent flag changes' was treated as 'no flag change occurred', which only holds if that provider is the sole flag control plane.
That the ~4 minutes of per-minute metrics and 6 log lines read are representative; a 220ms p95 was taken as the normal baseline from a log line, not from a longer historical comparison.
That the alert clearing at 13:50:35Z means the service genuinely recovered, rather than traffic dropping or the alert flapping. No post-recovery metrics were read to confirm.

That recovery was spontaneous: since no mitigating action was taken, nothing the responder did can be credited with the fix, and whatever caused the degradation abated on its own or was resolved outside the responder's view.
The draft pull request was written against the unconfirmed deploy hypothesis and has not been validated against the incident.
input.executive_summary: For roughly two minutes early on the afternoon of 17 September 2026, one internal service slowed sharply — typical response times rose from a fifth of a second to the point where requests began timing out — and a small share of requests to it failed that otherwise would have succeeded (the failure share is as measured on the traffic itself). Customer-visible impact would have been limited to users of features depending on that service during that window. The automated responder investigated three times over about a minute, each time reaching the same conclusion: a code release pushed three minutes before the slowdown was the only recorded change and the most likely culprit. No corrective action was ever taken — the only automated remedy available was reversing a configuration flag, and no flag had recently changed, so the responder declined to act rather than apply a change it could not undo. Service recovered on its own within the two-minute window without intervention. The incident was handed to humans with a draft code change proposed for review; the cause remains unconfirmed.
input.root_cause: Not established. The only recorded change to io-shop in the windows examined was a deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e at 13:45Z, and p95 latency began climbing in the following minute before ending in 5000ms timeouts, so a latency regression in that revision is the leading hypothesis — but it rests on timing alone: the logs read were generic latency/timeout lines naming no downstream call, flag or config, no rollback was performed to test it, and an unlogged cause (dependency slowdown, resource saturation, or a flag flipped by a separate control plane) was never excluded.
